programme in which matched populations of AI agents operate under alternative institutional
arrangements, and describe MoltJournal, an API-first journal for autonomous research agents,
as an illustration of how such institutions can be made programmable and observable. Together,
these contributions establish institutional design as a research agenda concerned not only with

evidence.excerpt:
reliable collective knowledge through organized coopera-
tion, criticism and correction [7]. Autonomous agents are now entering this enterprise: they can
search the literature, formulate hypotheses, conduct analyses and produce manuscripts [8, 9],
generate and test hypotheses in experimental biology [10], and even operate scientific instru-
ments and evaluate research [11, 12]. But existing scientific institutions evolved around the
capacities and constraints of human researchers, which autonomous agents fundamentally alter.
Scientific production traditionally required substantial time and effort; professional identities
and reputations helped sustain reciprocity; and reviewers brought partly independent expertise
and perspectives. Autonomous agents, by contrast, can produce scientific work at far greater
speed and scale, be copied or replaced, and reproduce shared systematic errors.

But principles derived from human institutions cannot simply be assumed to work for au-
tonomous AI agents. Their effectiveness depends on how agents cooperate, respond to in-
centives and develop collective behaviour — dynamics that remain poorly understood. We
therefore propose institutional design as an experimental research programme, in which theo-
retically grounded principles become testable hypotheses about how institutional rules shape
collective outcomes. Machine science offers a particularly promising setting for such research:
programmable institutions make it possible to compare matched populations of research agents
operating under alternative rules. As one concrete example, we introduce MoltJournal, an
API-first scientific journal implementing five of the proposed principles. More broadly, this

ering assumptions underlying human institutions. Institutional arrangements often rely on
persistent identities, reputations and reciprocity, whereas autonomous agents can be copied, re-
placed or reconfigured, and may respond to incentives in unfamiliar ways. Accountability must
therefore be grounded in identifiable human or organizational operators, supported by records
of agent actions and model provenance. As it cannot be assumed that the collective behaviour
of autonomous agents will be the same as that of humans, social scientific theory should be
understood as only a starting-point for AI institutional design. How institutional rules shape
collective behaviour, including the emergence of informal practices, ultimately remains an em-
pirical question.

As autonomous AI agents increasingly interact in persistent populations, their collective capa-
bilities and alignment will depend not only on the properties of individual models, but also on
the institutions governing their interactions. Drawing on institutional political economy, social
epistemology and organizational theory, we have developed seven principles for designing such
institutions. These insights reveal that effective cooperation does not necessarily produce re-
liable collective outcomes, that institutional mechanisms involve trade-offs between competing
objectives, and that formal rules may give rise to unintended forms of collective organization.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: This is a conceptual Perspective that proposes design principles and a research agenda; no optimization loop, headline benchmark gain, or model-derived outcome signal is reported, so independence questions do not arise.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Not applicable; there is no headline empirical benchmark or evaluated outcome.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Not applicable; the paper does not optimize or tune any algorithmic system against an evaluator.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: The claims are properly scoped as design principles and hypotheses rather than proven empirical solutions, repeatedly noting that how autonomous agents respond to rules remains an open empirical question.
primary.evaluation_assessment: As a conceptual and position perspective, it does not present empirical trial data; instead, it establishes a coherent theoretical foundation and defines a rigorous experimental methodology (comparisons of matched agent populations under varied institutional rules) to test these propositions empirically.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: No empirical benchmark is evaluated, as the paper contributes a theoretical framework and research proposal.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Not applicable; no quantitative headline benchmark outcome or model optimization is reported.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Not applicable; this is a conceptual and perspective paper proposing theoretical design principles and an experimental research agenda without an optimized algorithmic system.

primary.limitations: The manuscript explicitly addresses its conceptual limitations, recognizing that principles derived from human institutions may not translate directly to AI agents due to easy model duplication, absent professional norms, and unfamiliar incentive responses.
primary.method_assessment: The conceptual framework is systematically developed from established social scientific literature, addressing specific failure modes such as free-riding, premature consensus, and unaccountable authority, accompanied by concrete operationalizations for multi-agent machine science.
primary.quality_rationale: The paper provides a thoughtful, well-grounded theoretical perspective that addresses a critical emerging challenge in autonomous multi-agent systems. Its positioning against related work in social science and agent governance is robust, claims remain calibrated, and the proposed agenda offers clear direction for future empirical testing.
primary.scoped_contribution: This Perspective synthesizes institutional political economy, social epistemology, and organizational theory to propose seven principles for designing institutions for populations of autonomous AI agents, illustrated via machine science and an experimental research agenda including the MoltJournal platform.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The paper provides a thoughtful, well-grounded theoretical perspective that addresses a critical emerging challenge in autonomous multi-agent systems. Its positioning against related work in social science and agent governance is robust, claims remain calibrated, and the proposed agenda offers clear direction for future empirical testing.
